analysis.one_liner: Makes colleges with billion-dollar endowments pay a share of student costs and loan defaults.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The COLLEGE Act would require colleges that receive federal student aid and hold endowments over $1 billion to cover a share of each enrolled full-time student's cost of attendance — 25% for the smallest affected schools, rising to 75% for those with endowments over $10 billion. It would also make colleges repay an increasing share (up to 25%) of the federal loan balances of their former students who default, and require schools and the Education Department to publish detailed data on costs, graduation, employment, and debt by major.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at wealthy colleges stand to gain the most: the school itself would have to pay a quarter to three-quarters of their cost of attendance, which would cut what students and families pay or borrow. Students at all schools would get better information, because colleges would have to report graduation rates, post-graduation wages, and debt by major, and the Education Department would publish it. Taxpayers also gain, since colleges that leave students with high default rates would have to reimburse the government for part of the losses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students at colleges with big endowments

how_it_helps.text: Colleges with endowments over $1 billion must pay 25% of each full-time student's cost of attendance, rising to 50% for endowments over $5 billion and 75% for those over $10 billion — directly lowering what students and families pay at some of the most expensive schools [S3].

Schools must remit to the Education Department an increasing share of the loan balances of former students who default — starting at 1% and rising to 25% over 25 years — so colleges, not taxpayers, absorb part of the loss when their graduates can't repay [S3].

Every college receiving federal aid would have to report, by academic major, four-year graduation rates, employment and median wages of graduates 1, 3, and 5 years out, total degree cost, average loan payments, and average debt, and the Education Department must publish this data so prospective students can compare programs before enrolling [S3].
Schools must also report endowment size and four-quarter growth, distinguishing donations from investment returns, so students and the public can see how wealthy each institution is [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities with endowments over $1 billion pay the largest share — covering 25% to 75% of enrolled students' cost of attendance and repaying part of their graduates' defaulted federal loans. All colleges that participate in federal aid would bear the cost of collecting and reporting the new program-level data, and the Education Department would administer the new payments and reporting.

drawbacks.text: The cost-match mandate gives colleges a strong incentive to avoid the students who trigger the obligations — schools could respond by enrolling fewer low-income students who need federal aid or loans, the opposite of the bill's goal, since the requirements attach to every enrolled full-time student and to any borrower who defaults.

Endowments are often legally restricted: much of the money is donated for specific purposes like scholarships, professorships, or research, and the bill would require schools to pay a share of attendance costs regardless of whether their endowment funds are actually available for that use.

Risk-sharing payments reaching 25% of defaulted loan balances could push financially strained schools to drop federal loan participation altogether, cutting off access to safer federal loans for students who rely on them.

The bill defines cost of attendance to include living expenses, so a 75% mandate could exceed a wealthy school's tuition revenue and require dipping into restricted endowment principal, raising litigation and compliance costs that would fall partly on students.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students at wealthy schools, the potential tuition relief is large and the transparency provisions help students everywhere compare programs. But the design is blunt: it doesn't distinguish restricted from unrestricted endowment funds, applies the cost-match to every enrolled student rather than targeting aid to students with need, and creates a real risk that colleges respond by being choosier about low-income borrowers rather than by spending their endowments. The risk-sharing idea is sound in principle — colleges have long escaped consequences for poor graduation and default outcomes — but a 25% clawback on all defaulted balances is steep enough to have real side effects.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never voted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott introduced the COLLEGE Act on November 29, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP Committee that same day [S5].
The committee took no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill; it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the new Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and universities with endowments over $1 billion are better off: they keep their endowments untouched, pay nothing toward their students' costs, and bear none of the loan-default costs the bill would have shifted to them. Students at those schools get no tuition relief and remain the ones who pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthy colleges, which pay nothing now

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote of any kind, and it had zero cosponsors, so no record shows whether it would have split by party.

industries.industry: Private research universities with endowments over $1 billion (Ivy League, flagship private schools)
industries.note: The bill would force these institutions to pay 25%–75% of each enrolled student's cost of attendance and to reimburse up to 25% of their graduates' defaulted federal loans. Their interest in this bill ran directly against students' interest in lower costs, and the bill died without a vote, so they continue to pay nothing.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities generally (all federal-aid participants)
industries.note: Every federal-aid school would have to collect and report graduation, employment, wage, and debt data by major. That is a compliance cost for the industry but a transparency gain for prospective students; the schools would also lose the ability to obscure poor-performing programs behind institution-wide averages.

Taxpayers currently absorb nearly all losses when college borrowers default. The bill would shift up to 25% of those losses to the college the borrower attended, reducing the federal cost of defaults.
